title: A Million-Strong Bridge: How India's Diaspora Is Reshaping Australia's Strategic Calculus
excerpt: Australian High Commissioner Philip Green says the Indian community has become 'central to the bilateral architecture' as Canberra and New Delhi deepen ties in defence, trade and education
body:
When Philip Green, Australia's High Commissioner to India, describes the state of bilateral relations, he reaches not for the usual diplomatic bromides about "shared values" but for something more concrete: numbers. More than one million people of Indian origin now call Australia home. Some 135,000 Indian students are enrolled in Australian universities at any given time. Indians have overtaken the English as Australia's largest overseas-born population group. These are not footnotes in a diplomatic briefing; they are, Green argues, the very foundation on which the relationship now rests.

## From cricket to strategic calculus

The transformation has been swift. As recently as 2010, the India-Australia relationship was shadowed by a series of violent attacks on Indian students in Melbourne, which triggered a diplomatic freeze and a sharp drop in student enrolments. A decade and a half later, the dynamic could hardly be more different. The two countries are fellow members of the Quad, alongside the United States and Japan. They signed a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2020 and an Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement (ECTA) in 2022 — the latter already showing results, with Indian exports to Australia rising 4.4 per cent in its third year and bilateral trade touching $24 billion.

Green, speaking to Indian media this month, underscored that the relationship is now driven as much by the diaspora as by governments. Indian-origin Australians occupy senior positions in academia, medicine, technology and public life. Their remittances, investment flows and professional networks create a dense web of economic interdependence that formal treaties merely codify.

## The education pipeline

For many in the diaspora, education remains the primary gateway. Australia's universities — particularly the Group of Eight research-intensive institutions — draw Indian talent across engineering, data science, healthcare and business. The post-study work visa regime, which allows graduates to remain for two to four years depending on qualification level, has made Australia an increasingly attractive alternative to the United Kingdom, where tightening visa rules have dampened demand.

Yet the pipeline is not without friction. Recognition of Indian professional qualifications — particularly in medicine, engineering and accounting — remains patchy. Green acknowledged the gap, noting that work is under way to streamline mutual recognition frameworks as part of broader ECTA negotiations. For NRIs who trained in India and now practise in Australia, this is not an abstract policy question but a daily professional reality.

## Defence and the Indo-Pacific

Beyond trade and education, the strategic dimension of the relationship has deepened markedly. The tenth round of India-Australia Defence Policy Talks, held in New Delhi earlier this month, focused on maritime security, joint exercises including the Talisman Sabre series, and defence-industrial collaboration. A Joint Maritime Security Collaboration Roadmap is in preparation, reflecting shared anxieties about Chinese naval expansion in the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea.

For the Indian diaspora in Australia, this strategic convergence has a practical benefit: it cements their host country's commitment to a region in which India is a central actor, reducing the political risk of anti-immigrant sentiment that periodically flares in Australian public life.

## What comes next

The next milestone is the negotiation of a full Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement, which would go beyond ECTA to cover services, investment and labour mobility in greater depth. Green hinted that agricultural market access — long a sticking point — is edging closer to resolution, with tariff reductions on Australian lentils, almonds and wine already in effect.

For the million-strong Indian community in Australia, these developments are more than geopolitical abstractions. They are the policy infrastructure that determines whether a doctor trained in Hyderabad can practise in Sydney, whether a startup founder in Bengaluru can tap Australian venture capital, and whether a student from Patna can build a life on the other side of the Indian Ocean. The bridge, it seems, is only getting wider.
